title: Bēowulf
source: Fr. Klaeber, Beowulf and the Fight at Finnsburg, 1st edition (Boston: D. C. Heath & Co., 1922), pp. 42–45, lines 1125–1191 (fitt XVII). Text follows Klaeber's printing exactly — þ, ð, æ, vowel-length macrons, a circumflex for contracted vowels (Klaeber prints one mark over the pair of vowels; we place it on the second), [brackets] for letters or words added by emendation, (parentheses) for conjectural restoration of fire-damaged letters, and Klaeber's rows of dots where words are lost. A dot under a vowel (dōgọra) is Klaeber's sign that the vowel does not count in the metre. Transcribed from the page images of the archive.org scan, every page read twice. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed late West Saxon, c. 1000, following Campbell's Old English Grammar — and the recorded reading follows it, within stated limits. No synthetic voice for Old English exists, so the reading is produced by an American English neural voice under per-word phonetic pinning: every sound is specified outright rather than left to modern English habits. So æ is the vowel of 'cat' and a the open back vowel of 'father'; short and long vowels stay apart; ea and eo are sounded as two-part diphthongs; sc is 'sh', cg the 'j' of 'edge', hw a breathy w; h after a vowel is the rasp of German 'ach' or 'ich'; and doubled consonants are held long. The limits: the voice has no throaty g (dagas, lagu), so it says a plain g; long ǣ, long ȳ and long ēa are heard short; compounds are not split, so a sound at the seam of a compound is occasionally voiced where it should not be; and unstressed vowels keep their full quality. The reading is a model of one scholarly convention, as much a reconstruction as the text. Translations made fresh from the original.
about: Beowulf survives in a single manuscript, the Nowell Codex, which was scorched in a library fire in 1731; its edges have crumbled away, and some readings survive only in two transcripts made in 1787. What you read here is a reconstruction — Klaeber's edition of 1922 — and parts of it are educated guesswork: [brackets] mark letters editors added, (parentheses) mark letters restored where the manuscript is damaged or lost, and a few words are best guesses whose exact meaning no one knows. The notes say so where it matters. Line numbers are Klaeber's, the standard way of citing the poem.

sentences.t:
Gewiton him ðā wīgend wīca nēosian
frēondum befeallen, Frȳsland gesēon,
hāmas ond hēaburh.
sentences.l: Departed themselves then the warriors, to seek out the dwellings, fallen-away from friends, to see Frisland, homes and high-stronghold.
sentences.i: Then the warriors went their way, bereft of their friends, to seek out their dwellings and see Frisia, their homes and the high stronghold.
sentences.n: ‘Gewiton’ is the past plural of ‘gewītan’ (‘depart’), and ‘him’ is a reflexive dative, so ‘gewiton him’ is ‘went off’, ‘took themselves away’; ‘wīgend’ (‘warriors’, nominative plural) is the subject. ‘nēosian’ and ‘gesēon’ are infinitives of purpose, ‘to seek out’ and ‘to see’. ‘nēosian’ takes the genitive, so ‘wīca’ is genitive plural, ‘of dwellings’; ‘Frȳsland’, ‘hāmas’ (plural) and ‘hēaburh’ (singular, ‘high stronghold’) are accusatives after ‘gesēon’. ‘befeallen’ is the past participle of ‘befeallan’, ‘to fall away from, be deprived of’, and it takes the dative: ‘frēondum befeallen’ is ‘bereft of friends’, presumably the friends lost in the fighting told in the last fitt. The line does not name the warriors; because they go to Frisland, I take them as the surviving Frisians, which is a guess from the destination. Hengest and his Danes are left behind, as the next sentence says. The apparatus shows Holthausen and Schücking reading the shorter infinitive ‘nēosan’, which means the same.

sentences.l: Hengest then still a slaughter-stained winter dwelt with Finn, all unlotted;
sentences.i: Hengest then still spent that slaughter-stained winter with Finn, wholly in ill-luck;
sentences.n: ‘wintẹr’ has a dot under the ‘e’; this is Klaeber’s sign that the vowel does not count in the metre, and it changes nothing in the sense (the same mark appears again in ‘wuldọrtorhtan’, ‘wundẹrfatum’ and ‘umbọrwesendum’). Here ‘wintẹr’ is an accusative of duration, ‘for a winter’, with ‘wælfāgne’ (accusative singular masculine) agreeing with it; ‘wunode’ is the past singular of ‘wunian’, ‘dwell, stay’, and ‘mid Finne’ is ‘with Finn’. ‘Ðā gȳt’ is ‘then still’. ‘wælfāg’ is a compound of ‘wæl’ (the slain, slaughter) and ‘fāg’ (stained, coloured); I take it as ‘stained with slaughter’, a winter marked by the killing, which is a guess from the parts. The last half-line is damaged or corrupt. The manuscript reads ‘finnel unhlitme’, that is ‘Finne’ followed by a bare ‘l’; Klaeber inserts ‘ea’ in the brackets to make ‘eal’ (‘wholly, all’). Others read differently: Kemble ‘elne’ (courage), Heyne ‘ealles’, Thorkelin ‘unflitme’, Grein ‘ēðles’ (of the homeland), Kock ‘unhlīte’ (which he takes as ‘misfortune, exile’). ‘unhlitme’ itself occurs only here; ‘hlit’ is a lot (as in drawing lots), so ‘un-lotted’ would be ‘without good lot’, and ‘in ill-luck’ is a guess at the sense.

sentences.t:
eard gemunde,
þēah þe hē meahte on mere drīfan
hringedstefnan, —
sentences.l: He thought of home, though he could drive on the sea the ring-prowed one, —
sentences.i: he thought of his homeland, though he could drive his ring-prowed ship out on the sea, —
sentences.n: ‘eard’ is the accusative singular, ‘homeland, dwelling-place’, the object of ‘gemunde’ (past of ‘gemunan’, ‘remember, think of’); Hengest is still the subject. ‘þēah þe’ is ‘although’. ‘meahte’ is the past of ‘magan’ (‘can’) and has the same form in the indicative and the subjunctive. ‘on mere drīfan’ is ‘drive on the sea’, with ‘mere’ the noun ‘mere’ (sea, lake), whose accusative and dative are the same, so the case cannot be told from the form (‘on’ with motion would take the accusative) and ‘drīfan’ the infinitive. ‘hringedstefnan’ is the accusative of a weak noun ‘hringedstefna’, ‘ring-prowed one’, a compound of ‘hringed’ (ringed, fitted with rings) and ‘stefn’ (prow, stem), and it means a ship; why the prow is ‘ringed’ is not clear (rings of metal, or a curved prow), and I leave the picture as the word gives it. Many editors, and the apparatus lists Grundtvig first, add ‘[ne]’ before ‘meahte’, so that the sentence says he could not sail; Klaeber keeps the manuscript, so ‘he could sail but did not’, and the storm in the next sentence then tells what stood in the way. The dash joins the next sentence.

sentences.t:
holm storme wēol,
won wið winde, wintẹr ȳþe belēac
īsgebinde, oþ ðæt ōþer cōm
gēar in geardas, —
sentences.l: the sea surged with storm, strove against the wind, winter locked the waves with ice-binding, until another year came into the dwellings, —
sentences.i: the sea surged with storm and strove against the wind; winter locked the waves fast in bonds of ice, until another year came round to the dwellings of men, —
sentences.n: The subjects are ‘holm’ (sea, nominative) and ‘wintẹr’ (nominative this time, after the accusative in the last unit). ‘storme’ is dative, ‘with storm’; ‘wēol’ is the past of ‘weallan’, ‘to surge, boil’; ‘won’ is the past of ‘winnan’, ‘to strive’, with ‘wið winde’, ‘against the wind’. ‘ȳþe’ is the accusative plural of ‘ȳþ’ (wave), the object of ‘belēac’ (past of ‘belūcan’, ‘lock up, shut in’), and ‘īsgebinde’ is a dative, ‘with ice-binding’: ‘gebind’ is a binding, fastening, and the compound makes the ice a chain laid on the water. ‘oþ ðæt’ is ‘until’; ‘ōþer … gēar’ is ‘another year’ (nominative singular neuter) with ‘cōm’ (past of ‘cuman’) and ‘in geardas’, ‘into the dwellings’ (accusative plural of ‘geard’, enclosure, yard, dwelling-place). The year is spoken of as a visitor that comes, so ‘came round’ in the idiomatic version is mine. The dash leads into the poet’s remark about his own day.

sentences.t:
swā nū gȳt dêð,
þā ðe syngāles sēle bewitiað,
wuldọrtorhtan weder.
sentences.l: as now still it does, those who continually the seasons observe, the glory-bright weather.
sentences.i: as still happens in our own day with those who keep unbroken watch on the seasons, the bright and glorious weather.
sentences.n: This is a hard sentence, and my version is a smoothing of it. ‘swā nū gȳt dêð’ is ‘as it now still does’; the circumflex in ‘dêð’ marks a contracted vowel (it is the present of ‘dōn’, ‘do’), and the verb is singular, as if the year were its subject. ‘þā ðe … bewitiað’ is ‘those who observe’ and is plural, so the printed text puts a singular verb beside a plural subject. The apparatus lists the repairs: Thorkelin ‘dōð’ and Aant., Holthausen and Schücking ‘dōað’ (plural, ‘as those do who…’), Grein and Sedgefield ‘dēð’ with ‘þām ðe’ (‘as it does for those who…’). Klaeber leaves the manuscript form. ‘syngāles’ is an adverb, ‘continually’; ‘bewitiað’ is the present plural of ‘bewitian’, ‘watch over, observe’. ‘sēle’ is spelled with a long ‘ē’, and I take it as the accusative plural of ‘sǣl’ in the sense ‘times, seasons’, which is a guess. ‘wuldọrtorhtan weder’ is ‘glory-bright weather’ (‘wuldor’ glory, ‘torht’ bright), in apposition to ‘sēle’. The poet, speaking in his own time, says that the year still turns as it did then.

sentences.t:
Ðā wæs winter scacen,
fæger foldan bearm;
sentences.l: Then was winter departed, fair the bosom of the earth;
sentences.i: Then winter was gone, and the lap of the earth was fair;
sentences.n: ‘wæs scacen’ is ‘was gone’: ‘scacen’ is the past participle of ‘scacan’ (‘shake, go away’), and ‘wesan’ with the participle makes the perfect for verbs of motion. ‘fæger foldan bearm’ has no verb and stands beside the first clause: ‘fæger’ (fair) is the nominative, ‘bearm’ (lap, bosom) the subject, and ‘foldan’ the genitive singular ‘of the earth’. The bosom of the earth is the ground in spring.

sentences.t:
fundode wrecca,
gist of geardum;
sentences.l: the exile hastened, the guest, from the dwellings;
sentences.i: the exile made ready to be gone, the stranger leaving the dwellings;
sentences.n: ‘fundode’ is the past of ‘fundian’, ‘to hasten, strive to go’, and ‘wrecca’ (‘exile, one driven out’, nominative) is its subject, here Hengest, who is far from his own land. ‘gist’ is in apposition and is a spelling of ‘gæst’, ‘guest, stranger’ (the long-vowelled ‘gāst’, ghost, is another word). ‘of geardum’ is ‘from the dwellings’, the dative plural after ‘of’. Whether he means to leave Finn’s hall for the sea or only to leave the winter quarters is not said; the next unit gives his mind.

sentences.t:
hē tō gyrnwræce
swīðor þōhte þonne tō sǣlāde,
gif hē torngemōt þurhtēon mihte,
þæt hē Ēotena bearn inne gemunde.
sentences.l: he of grief-vengeance more thought than of the sea-way, if he a hostile meeting could carry through, that he the Eotens’ son(s) within remembered.
sentences.i: His thoughts ran more on revenge for his wrongs than on the voyage, if he could only bring about a hostile meeting, so that he might bear in mind the sons of the Eotens, within.
sentences.n: ‘swīðor’ is the comparative adverb, ‘more strongly, rather’; ‘þōhte’ (past of ‘þencan’) takes ‘tō’ with the dative, so ‘tō gyrnwræce … þonne tō sǣlāde’ is ‘of revenge rather than of the sea-way’. ‘gyrnwræc’ is a compound of ‘gyrn’ (grief, injury) and ‘wræc’ (vengeance, punishment): vengeance for a wrong done. ‘sǣlād’ is ‘sea-way’, sea-crossing. ‘gif hē … þurhtēon mihte’ is ‘if he could carry through’ (past tense with a hypothetical sense, ‘if he were able’; ‘mihte’ has the same form in the indicative and the subjunctive), the object being ‘torngemōt’, ‘hostile meeting’, a compound of ‘torn’ (anger) and ‘gemōt’ (meeting) meaning a battle. The last clause is uncertain. ‘þæt hē … gemunde’ is ‘that he remembered’ (past tense of ‘gemunan’, in form either indicative or subjunctive), the object ‘Ēotena bearn’, ‘the sons of the Eotens’ (‘bearn’ is the same in singular and plural), and ‘inne’ is ‘within’, ‘inside’. The apparatus lists many emendations (Thorkelin ‘þæs’, Sievers and Holthausen ‘þǣr hē’, Cosijn and Sedgefield ‘þæt hē [wið]’, Rieger ‘bearnum’ with ‘gemynte’, Trautmann ‘īrne’ for ‘inne’), which shows how little is agreed. My reading takes ‘remember’ as ‘keep in mind, so as to requite’, and ‘inne’ as ‘within’ in the sense ‘indoors’ or ‘inwardly’; both are guesses. Who the Eotens are is disputed (see the last fitt, line 1071); I take them, there and here, as Finn’s side of the quarrel.

sentences.l: So he did not refuse the world-custom, when Hunlafing the battle-light, best of swords, laid on his lap;
sentences.i: So he did not refuse the custom of the world, when Hunlafing laid the battle-light, the best of swords, in his lap;
sentences.n: ‘forwyrnde’ is the past of ‘forwyrnan’, ‘to refuse, deny’, and its object is ‘woroldrǣdenne’, accusative singular of ‘woroldrǣden’, ‘world-condition, worldly custom’ (‘worold’ world, ‘rǣden’ rule, condition). This phrase is disputed: Möller (‘Mo.’), Bugge and Sedgefield read ‘worodrǣdenne’, ‘troop-condition, the duty of the band’, and Schücking takes the whole line as a subordinate clause. I take it as the usual duty that falls on a man whose lord was killed, namely vengeance, which is a guess. ‘þonne’ is ‘when’; ‘him’ is dative, ‘to him’; ‘Hūnlāfing’ is either the son of Hunlaf (the ending ‘-ing’ is ‘son of’) or, as Bugge and Trautmann print, two words, a man ‘Hun’ the ‘Lafing’; the poem gives no more. ‘hildelēoman’ is the accusative of ‘hildelēoma’, ‘battle-light’, a poetic name for a sword (Holthausen prints it with a capital, as the sword’s name), and ‘billa sēlest’ is ‘best of swords’ (genitive plural ‘billa’, superlative ‘sēlest’). ‘on bearm dyde’ is ‘put on the lap’, ‘dyde’ being the past of ‘dōn’. To lay a sword in a man’s lap is evidently a summons to act, and here to avenge, though the text does not explain the gesture.

sentences.t: þæs wǣron mid Ēotenum ecge cūðe.
sentences.l: Of it were among the Eotens the edges known.
sentences.i: Its edges were well known among the Eotens.
sentences.n: ‘þæs’ is the genitive singular of ‘se’, ‘of that’, referring to the sword just named; ‘ecge’ is the nominative plural of ‘ecg’ (edge, blade), and ‘cūðe’ is the nominative plural of ‘cūþ’ (known, familiar). So ‘þæs wǣron … ecge cūðe’ is ‘of it the edges were known’, with ‘mid Ēotenum’, ‘among the Eotens’, saying who knew them: they had felt it in the fighting. The sense hangs on the last unit, since the sword is the one laid in Hengest’s lap.

sentences.t:
Swylce ferhðfrecan Fin eft begeat
sweordbealo slīðen æt his selfes hām,
sentences.l: Likewise sword-evil, fierce, seized the bold-spirited Finn in turn, at his own home,
sentences.i: So in his turn fierce slaughter by the sword overtook the stout-hearted Finn in his own home,
sentences.n: ‘swylce’ is ‘likewise’; ‘eft’ is ‘again, in turn’. ‘begeat’ is the past singular of ‘begitan’, ‘to get hold of, seize, befall’, and it takes an accusative object: ‘ferhðfrecan Fin’ (accusative singular masculine, ‘the bold-spirited Finn’; ‘ferhð’ spirit, ‘frec’ bold, greedy). The thing that seized him is the subject, ‘sweordbealo’ (‘sword-evil’, nominative neuter, a compound of ‘sweord’ sword and ‘bealo’ evil, harm) with ‘slīðen’ (‘fierce, cruel’, nominative neuter, agreeing). The literal version puts ‘sword-evil’ first, although it stands second in the Old English, because the order of the Old English does not by itself show a modern reader that Finn is the object; the idiomatic version says ‘slaughter by the sword overtook him’. ‘æt his selfes hām’ is ‘at his own home’ (‘selfes’ genitive singular, ‘of himself’). The sentence tells that the peace Finn swore was answered in kind, in his own hall.

sentences.l: after, the grim grip Guthlaf and Oslaf, after the sea-journey, in sorrow lamented, reproached a share of woes;
sentences.i: after Guthlaf and Oslaf, once the sea-voyage was over, had lamented in sorrow the fierce assault, and reproached him with a share of the woes;
sentences.n: ‘siþðan’ is ‘after’. ‘siþðan’ opens a clause whose verbs are ‘mǣndon’ (past plural of ‘mǣnan’, ‘lament, complain of’) and ‘ætwiton’ (past plural of ‘ætwītan’, ‘reproach, taunt’), with ‘Gūðlāf ond Ōslāf’ as the subject; I take the clause as saying what came before Finn’s death in the sentence above. ‘grimne gripe’ is the accusative singular masculine of ‘grim gripe’, ‘fierce grip’, that is the fierce attack, the attack in which Hnæf fell (told in the last fitt); ‘sorge’ is ‘sorrow’ (accusative and dative are alike), which I take as ‘in sorrow’, and ‘æfter sǣsīðe’ is ‘after the sea-journey’, perhaps the voyage that brought Hnæf’s party to Finn’s hall. The two names are new in this part, and the text gives them no more than their grief; I take them as Danes of the surviving band. ‘ætwiton wēana dǣl’ is ‘reproached a share of woes’, where ‘dǣl’ is the accusative singular and ‘wēana’ the genitive plural of ‘wēa’, ‘woe’; the person reproached is not named and has to be Finn, which is a guess from what follows.

sentences.t:
ne meahte wǣfre mōd
forhabban in hreþre.
sentences.l: not could the restless spirit hold itself back in the breast.
sentences.i: Their restless spirit could not hold back in the breast.
sentences.n: ‘ne meahte’ is ‘could not’. ‘wǣfre mōd’ is the subject: ‘mōd’ is neuter, ‘spirit, mind, mood’, and ‘wǣfre’ (‘restless, unsteady’) agrees with it; the ending is not the usual one for a neuter nominative singular, which would be ‘wǣfer’, so the agreement is a little irregular, but no other reading suggests itself. ‘forhabban’ is the infinitive ‘to hold back, restrain’ with no object stated, so it means ‘restrain itself’, and ‘in hreþre’ is ‘in the breast’ (dative of ‘hreþer’). The sentence says what the reproach led to: their anger would no longer stay inside. The verb is ‘meahte’, singular, though the two men are the subject of the sentence before; the ‘mōd’ is one, the shared spirit of the pair.

sentences.t:
Ðā wæs heal roden
fēonda fēorum, swilce Fin slægen,
cyning on corþre, ond sēo cwēn numen.
sentences.l: Then was the hall reddened with the lives of foes, likewise Finn slain, the king in the troop, and the queen taken.
sentences.i: Then the hall was reddened with the lifeblood of foes; Finn too was slain, the king among his troop, and the queen was taken captive.
sentences.n: ‘Ðā wæs heal roden’ is ‘then was the hall reddened’: ‘roden’ is the past participle of ‘rēodan’, ‘to redden’, and Klaeber’s italic ‘r’ shows his alteration of the manuscript, which has ‘hroden’ (the participle of ‘hrēodan’, ‘adorn’, which would give ‘adorned with the lives of foes’); Bugge’s ‘roden’ is accepted for the sense. ‘fēonda fēorum’ is ‘with the lives of foes’: ‘fēorum’ is the dative plural of ‘feorh’ (life), ‘fēonda’ the genitive plural of ‘fēond’. ‘swilce’ is ‘likewise’; ‘Fin slægen’ and ‘sēo cwēn numen’ need ‘wæs’ from the first clause, and ‘slægen’ (slain) and ‘numen’ (taken) are past participles of ‘slēan’ and ‘niman’. ‘cyning on corþre’ is ‘the king in the troop’ (‘corþre’ is the dative of ‘corþor’, a band of men). The queen is Hildeburh, who had lost her son and brother in the first fighting, and who is now taken away from Finn.

sentences.t:
Scēotend Scyldinga tō scypon feredon
eal ingesteald eorðcyninges,
swylce hīe æt Finnes hām findan meahton
sigla searogimma.
sentences.l: The shooters of the Scyldings to the ships bore all the in-furnishing of the earth-king, such as they at Finn’s home could find of brooches, of cunning-gems.
sentences.i: The Scylding warriors carried to the ships all the household treasure of the king of the land, whatever brooches and cunningly wrought jewels they could find in Finn’s home.
sentences.n: ‘Scēotend’ is ‘shooters’, a poetic word for warriors, in the nominative plural, with ‘Scyldinga’ the genitive plural, ‘of the Scyldings’. ‘feredon’ is the past plural of ‘ferian’, ‘to carry’; ‘tō scypon’ is ‘to the ships’ (dative plural). ‘eal ingesteald’ is the accusative singular neuter, ‘all the household goods’ (‘ingesteald’, the stock within the house), and ‘eorðcyninges’ is the genitive singular of ‘eorðcyning’, ‘earth-king’, a king over a land and its people, so ‘king of the land’ in the idiomatic version. ‘swylce’ here introduces ‘such as’, and Trautmann and Holthausen read ‘swylc’ to make that plain. ‘sigla’ is the genitive plural of ‘sigel’ (a brooch, jewel; the same word also means ‘sun’) and ‘searogimma’ the genitive plural of ‘searogimm’ (‘cunning-gem’, ‘searo’ being skill or craft): both depend on the ‘swylce’ clause as ‘of brooches, of cunning-gems’, naming the sort of things found.

sentences.t:
Hīe on sǣlāde
drihtlīce wīf tō Denum feredon,
lǣddon tō lēodum.
sentences.l: They on the sea-way noble-like woman to the Danes bore, led to the people.
sentences.i: They bore the noble lady over the sea to the Danes, and led her back to her own people.
sentences.n: ‘Hīe’ is ‘they’, the Scylding warriors; ‘feredon’ and ‘lǣddon’ (past plural of ‘lǣdan’, ‘lead’) are the two verbs, the second saying the same in other words, with the woman as the object of both. ‘on sǣlāde’ is ‘on the sea-way’. The woman is Hildeburh, the queen who had been ‘taken’ in the last unit; ‘wīf’ is a neuter noun (‘woman’, accusative singular). ‘drihtlīce’ is either an adjective, ‘noble, lordly’, agreeing with ‘wīf’, or an adverb with ‘feredon’, ‘nobly’. The ending ‘-e’ is the regular adverb ending, and beside a neuter noun an adjective would normally have none, so the adverb is the likelier form on grammar alone; I nevertheless render it as an adjective, a guess, and the sense changes little. ‘tō Denum’ is ‘to the Danes’ and ‘tō lēodum’ is ‘to the people’ (both dative plural), her own people, since she was Hoc’s daughter and Hnæf’s sister, as the last fitt tells.

sentences.t:
Lēoð wæs āsungen,
glēomannes gyd.
sentences.l: The song was sung out, the gleeman’s lay.
sentences.i: The song was sung to its end, the minstrel’s tale.
sentences.n: ‘Lēoð’ (song, lay, nominative neuter) is the subject, and ‘wæs āsungen’ is the passive, ‘was sung out’, ‘sung through to the end’: the prefix ‘ā-’ gives the sense of completion. ‘glēomannes gyd’ is in apposition, ‘the gleeman’s tale’ (‘glēomannes’ genitive singular, ‘gyd’ nominative neuter, ‘lay, tale’). This sentence is the poet’s signal that the story of Finn, announced at line 1066, is finished. The hall’s ordinary noise returns in the next unit.

sentences.t:
Gamen eft āstāh,
beorhtode bencswēg, byrelas sealdon
wīn of wundẹrfatum.
sentences.l: Mirth again mounted, brightened the bench-noise, cupbearers gave wine from wonder-vessels.
sentences.i: Merriment rose again; the din of the benches rang out, and the cupbearers poured wine from wondrous vessels.
sentences.n: ‘Gamen’ (mirth, nominative neuter) is the subject of ‘āstāh’ (past singular of ‘āstīgan’, ‘climb, rise’), and ‘eft’ is ‘again’. ‘beorhtode’ is the past of ‘beorhtian’, whose basic sense is ‘to shine, be bright’; of a sound it must mean ‘rang clear’, and that carry-over of sense is my guess. Sedgefield would read ‘beorhtmode’, from ‘bearhtm’ (noise), which would make the sense ‘the bench-noise sounded’. ‘bencswēg’ is ‘bench-noise’ (‘benc’ bench, ‘swēg’ sound), the sound of the company on the benches. ‘byrelas’ is the nominative plural of ‘byrele’, ‘cupbearer’; ‘sealdon’ is the past plural of ‘sellan’, ‘give’, and ‘wīn’ is the object. ‘of wundẹrfatum’ is ‘from wonder-vessels’, the dative plural of ‘wundorfæt’ (‘wundor’ wonder, ‘fæt’ vessel), meaning vessels of marvellous workmanship; the dot under the ‘ẹ’ is again Klaeber’s metrical sign.

sentences.l: Then came Wealhtheow forth, going under a golden ring, where the two good ones sat, uncle and nephew;
sentences.i: Then Wealhtheow came forward, walking under her golden circlet, to where the two good men sat, uncle and nephew;
sentences.n: ‘cwōm’ is the past of ‘cuman’, ‘came’, and ‘gān’ the infinitive ‘to go, walk’, so ‘cwōm … gān’ is ‘came walking’. ‘Wealhþēo’ is the nominative, Hrothgar’s queen (the final ‘w’ of ‘Wealhþēow’ is missing, as before). ‘under gyldnum bēage’ is ‘under a golden ring’, the dative singular of ‘bēag’, ‘ring, circlet’: she wears a gold band on her head. ‘þǣr’ is ‘where’, ‘þā gōdan twēgen’ is ‘the two good ones’ (nominative plural masculine, ‘twēgen’ being the masculine ‘two’), and ‘sǣton’ is the past plural of ‘sittan’. ‘suhtergefæderan’ is the nominative plural of a rare compound in apposition; it names two kinsmen, uncle and nephew, and I take it as ‘paternal uncle and nephew’, which fits the two men named in fitt XV, Hrothgar and Hrothulf. The exact breakdown of the word is a guess.

sentences.t:
þā gȳt wæs hiera sib ætgædere,
ǣghwylc ōðrum trȳwe.
sentences.l: then still was their kinship together, each to the other true.
sentences.i: The bond between them still held at that time, each true to the other.
sentences.n: ‘þā gȳt’ is ‘still at that time’, and ‘wæs hiera sib ætgædere’ is ‘their kinship (or peace) was together’: ‘sib’ is the nominative singular feminine, ‘kinship, peace’, and ‘hiera’ the genitive plural ‘of them’. ‘ǣghwylc ōðrum trȳwe’ is ‘each to the other true’, with ‘ǣghwylc’ (each) in the nominative, ‘ōðrum’ (the other) in the dative, and ‘trȳwe’ (true, faithful) in the nominative. The word ‘gȳt’ (‘still’) implies that the bond lay under threat, but the poet says no more here.

sentences.t:
Swylce þǣr Unferþ þyle
æt fōtum sæt frēan Scyldinga;
sentences.l: Likewise there Unferth, the spokesman, sat at the feet of the lord of the Scyldings;
sentences.i: And Unferth, the king’s spokesman, sat there too, at the feet of the lord of the Scyldings;
sentences.n: ‘Swylce’ is ‘likewise, also’. The italic ‘Un’ is Klaeber’s alteration: the manuscript has two separate words ‘hun ferþ’, and Rieger read them as the name; the same man was named at line 499 as the one who sat ‘æt fōtum’ of the king. ‘þyle’ is the nominative singular of ‘þyle’, ‘spokesman, orator’, the court officer who speaks for the king. ‘æt fōtum’ is ‘at the feet’ (dative plural), and ‘frēan Scyldinga’ is ‘of the lord of the Scyldings’ (‘frēan’ dative singular of ‘frēa’, ‘Scyldinga’ genitive plural); that is Hrothgar. Unferth is the man who taunted Beowulf at the feast in fitts VIII and IX.

sentences.t:
gehwylc hiora his ferhþe trēowde,
þæt hē hæfde mōd micel, þēah þe hē his māgum nǣre
ārfæst æt ecga gelācum.
sentences.l: each of them trusted his spirit, that he had a great mind, though he to his kinsmen was not honourable at the sword-play.
sentences.i: each of them trusted in his spirit, that he had a great heart, even though he was not merciful to his own kinsmen in the play of swords.
sentences.n: ‘gehwylc hiora’ is ‘each of them’ (‘hiora’ genitive plural). ‘trēowde’ is the past of ‘trēowian’, ‘to trust’, which takes the dative, so ‘his ferhþe’ is ‘in his spirit’; I take ‘his’ as Unferth’s, so that everyone trusted his courage, but the line could also mean that each man trusted his own. ‘þæt hē hæfde mōd micel’ says what they trusted: ‘that he had great courage’ (‘mōd’ accusative, ‘micel’ great). ‘þēah þe hē … nǣre’ is ‘though he were not’, where ‘nǣre’ is ‘ne wǣre’, the past subjunctive of ‘bēon’ with the negative joined to it. ‘ārfæst’ means ‘honourable, merciful’ (from ‘ār’, honour, mercy), ‘māgum’ is the dative plural ‘to kinsmen’, and ‘æt ecga gelācum’ is ‘at the play of edges’, that is at sword-fighting (‘gelācum’ dative plural of ‘gelāc’, play, sport). The words point back to Beowulf’s charge against him in fitt IX (line 587 and following) that he had killed his own brothers.

sentences.t: Spræc ðā ides Scyldinga:
sentences.l: Spoke then the lady of the Scyldings:
sentences.i: Then the lady of the Scyldings spoke:
sentences.n: ‘Spræc’ is the past singular of ‘sprecan’, ‘speak’, and ‘ides’ (‘lady’, nominative) is Wealhtheow, called by a title as Hildeburh was in the last fitt. ‘Scyldinga’ is the genitive plural, ‘of the Scyldings’. This is the plain verb of speaking; the formula ‘maþelode’ is not used here. The colon announces her speech.

sentences.t:
‘Onfōh þissum fulle, frēodrihten mīn,
sinces brytta!
sentences.l: ‘Receive this cup, my free-lord, treasure’s dispenser!
sentences.i: ‘Take this cup, my lord, giver of treasure!
sentences.n: ‘Onfōh’ is the imperative singular of ‘onfōn’, ‘to receive, take’, and the cup is in the dative, ‘þissum fulle’ (‘this cup’, dative singular), since ‘onfōn’ takes that case. ‘frēodrihten mīn’ is a vocative: ‘frēo’ (free, noble) and ‘drihten’ (lord) make ‘lord’ with the sense of a lord who is free-born and a protector of his people; ‘mīn’ is ‘my’. ‘sinces brytta’ is the vocative ‘dispenser of treasure’: ‘sinces’ is the genitive of ‘sinc’, treasure, and ‘brytta’ is the weak noun ‘distributor’, the old name for a generous lord. The queen carries the cup round the hall, as she did for Beowulf in fitt IX.

sentences.t:
Þū on sǣlum wes,
goldwine gumena, ond tō Gēatum spræc
mildum wordum, swā sceal man dôn!
sentences.l: You be in joys, gold-friend of men, and to the Geats speak with mild words, so shall one do!
sentences.i: Be glad, gold-friend of men, and speak to the Geats in gentle words; that is what a man should do!
sentences.n: ‘Þū on sǣlum wes’ is ‘be in joys’: ‘wes’ is the imperative of ‘wesan’ (the verb ‘bēon’ supplies the imperative ‘bēo’ in the next sentence), and ‘on sǣlum’ is ‘in happiness’ (dative plural of ‘sǣl’, ‘happiness, good fortune’). ‘goldwine gumena’ is a vocative, ‘gold-friend of men’: ‘goldwine’ is a ‘friend who gives gold’, a kenning for a generous lord, and ‘gumena’ is the genitive plural ‘of men’. ‘spræc’ is formally the past singular of ‘sprecan’, since the imperative would be ‘sprec’, and the sentence could be read as a report: ‘and you spoke to the Geats in mild words’, with ‘swā sceal man dôn’ praising what he did. I take it as an imperative, because the next sentence is also a command, and I call this a guess. ‘mildum wordum’ is dative plural, ‘with mild words’. ‘swā sceal man dôn’ is ‘so shall (so ought) one do’; ‘man’ is the indefinite ‘one’, ‘dôn’ is the infinitive of ‘dōn’ with a circumflex, Klaeber’s mark for a contracted vowel.

sentences.t:
Bēo wið Gēatas glæd, geofena gemyndig,
nēan ond feorran þū nū hafast.
sentences.l: Be glad toward the Geats, mindful of gifts; from near and from far you now have —
sentences.i: Be kind to the Geats, and remember gifts; from near and far you now have —
sentences.n: ‘Bēo’ is the imperative of ‘bēon’, ‘be’, ‘wið Gēatas’ is ‘toward the Geats’ (accusative plural after ‘wið’), and ‘glæd’ is ‘glad, gracious’ (nominative singular masculine). ‘geofena gemyndig’ is ‘mindful of gifts’: ‘gemyndig’ takes the genitive, and ‘geofena’ is the genitive plural of ‘giefu’, ‘gift’; the thought is that he should give gifts to the guests who have served him. The second line is incomplete. ‘nēan ond feorran’ is ‘from near and from far’ (adverbs), and ‘þū nū hafast’ is ‘you now have’, but the verb has no object. The apparatus shows the difficulty: some editors add a word (‘E.Sc.’ and others ‘[friðu]’, ‘peace’; Trautmann ‘[þā]’ or ‘[þē]’ and Sedgefield ‘[þē]’; Sievers ‘[þē]’ with a gap before the line; Bugge a whole extra half-line), and Rieger changes the reading to ‘nȳd hafast’ (‘you have need’) with a stop after ‘feorran’. I do not choose between them, and my versions leave the gap open, which is itself a guess about what the line meant.

sentences.t:
Mē man sægde, þæt þū ðē for sunu wolde
hereri[n]c habban.
sentences.l: To me one said that you for yourself as son would a warrior have.
sentences.i: I was told that you wished to take the warrior as a son for yourself.
sentences.n: ‘Mē man sægde’ is ‘to me one said’, that is, ‘I was told’, with ‘man’ the indefinite ‘one’ and ‘mē’ dative. The reported content is ‘þæt þū … wolde … habban’: ‘wolde’ is the past of ‘willan’ (‘wished, would’; the form is the same in the indicative and the subjunctive, and reported speech suggests the subjunctive), and ‘habban’ the infinitive ‘to have’. ‘ðē’ is a reflexive dative, ‘for yourself’, and ‘for sunu’ is ‘as a son’ (‘for’ with the accusative has this sense). The word ‘hereri[n]c’ is Kemble’s: the manuscript has ‘here ric’, two separate words, and Kemble supplies the ‘n’ to give ‘hererinc’, ‘army-man, warrior’ (accusative singular), compare line 2466, where the manuscript has ‘heaðo ri͏̊c’ for ‘heaðorinc’. The warrior is Beowulf, to whom Hrothgar said at line 946 that he would love him as a son.

sentences.t:
Heorot is gefǣlsod,
bēahsele beorhta;
sentences.l: Heorot is cleansed, the ring-hall bright;
sentences.i: Heorot is cleansed, the bright hall where rings are given;
sentences.n: ‘is gefǣlsod’ is ‘has been cleansed’: ‘gefǣlsod’ is the past participle of ‘gefǣlsian’, with ‘is’ to make the perfect. The cleansing is the clearing of Grendel from the hall. ‘bēahsele’ is the nominative of ‘bēahsele’, ‘ring-hall’, a compound of ‘bēah’ (ring) and ‘sele’ (hall); the hall is so named because the lord gives rings there. ‘beorhta’ is ‘bright’, in the weak nominative singular masculine, agreeing with ‘bēahsele’, which stands in apposition to ‘Heorot’.

sentences.t:
brūc þenden þū mōte
manigra mēdo, ond þīnum māgum lǣf
folc ond rīce, þonne ðū forð scyle,
metodsceaft seôn.
sentences.l: Enjoy, while you may, many rewards, and to your kinsmen leave people and kingdom, when you shall go forth to see the Measurer’s decree.
sentences.i: Enjoy many rewards while you may, and leave to your kinsmen the people and the kingdom, when you must go forth to meet your appointed end.
sentences.n: ‘brūc’ and ‘lǣf’ are imperatives singular, ‘enjoy’ and ‘leave’. ‘brūcan’ takes the genitive, so ‘manigra mēdo’ is ‘of many … (rewards)’; ‘manigra’ is the genitive plural of ‘manig’. The second word is in doubt: the manuscript has ‘medo’, which could be ‘mēd’, ‘reward’, in a genitive plural form with an unusual ending; Kemble reads ‘mēda’, Grein ‘māðma’ (treasures), Trautmann ‘mērða’ (glories), and I take it as ‘rewards’, which is a guess. ‘þenden’ is ‘while’. ‘þīnum māgum’ is the dative ‘to your kinsmen’, and ‘folc ond rīce’ (‘people and kingdom’) the accusative objects of ‘lǣf’. ‘þonne ðū forð scyle’ is ‘when you shall go forth’, that is die. ‘metodsceaft seôn’ is ‘to see the Measurer’s decree’: ‘Metod’ is God, ‘Measurer’ as in the house rendering, ‘sceaft’ is what is shaped or ordained, and ‘seôn’ (circumflex for the contracted vowel) is the infinitive of ‘sēon’; to ‘see’ it is to meet one’s death. I read it as a gentle way of saying die.

sentences.t:
Ic mīnne can
glædne Hrōþulf, þæt hē þā geogoðe wile
ārum healdan, gyf þū ǣr þonne hē,
wine Scildinga, worold oflǣtest;
sentences.l: I my gracious Hrothulf know, that he the youth will with honours hold, if you earlier than he, friend of the Scyldings, leave the world;
sentences.i: I know that my gracious Hrothulf will treat the young ones with kindness, if you, friend of the Scyldings, leave the world before he does;
sentences.n: ‘Ic … can’ is ‘I know’ (first singular of ‘cunnan’), and the accusative ‘mīnne … glædne Hrōþulf’ is ‘my gracious Hrothulf’; the sentence says ‘I know Hrothulf, that he will…’. ‘glæd’ means ‘glad’ or ‘gracious’. ‘þæt hē … wile … healdan’ is ‘that he will hold’: ‘wile’ is ‘wishes to, will’, and ‘þā geogoðe’ is the accusative, ‘the young’, the young men and boys of the court, presumably her own sons above all. ‘ārum’ is ‘with honours’ (dative plural of ‘ār’, ‘honour, kindness, mercy’). ‘gyf þū ǣr þonne hē … worold oflǣtest’ is ‘if you leave the world sooner than he’, with ‘oflǣtest’ the second-person singular of ‘oflǣtan’, ‘to give up, leave’; ‘wine Scildinga’ (‘friend of the Scyldings’, vocative) is an address to Hrothgar inside the clause. Hrothulf is Hrothgar’s nephew, the younger of the ‘uncle and nephew’ whom the unit at line 1162 (Wealhtheow’s entrance) leaves unnamed, and so the man in whose hands the queen’s sons would be left.

sentences.t:
wēne ic þæt hē mid gōde gyldan wille
uncran eaferan, gif hē þæt eal gemon,
hwæt wit tō willan ond tō worðmyndum
umbọrwesendum ǣr ārna gefremedon.’
sentences.l: I expect that he with good repay our two’s offspring, if he all that remembers, what we two for his pleasure and honours, when he was a child, earlier of kindnesses did.’
sentences.i: I expect that he will repay our children with good, if he remembers all that we two did for his pleasure and his honour in kindness, when he was a child.’
sentences.n: ‘wēne ic’ is ‘I expect, I think’ (first singular of ‘wēnan’), and ‘þæt hē … gyldan wille’ is ‘that he will repay’; ‘mid gōde’ is ‘with good’. ‘uncran eaferan’ uses the dual: Old English has a ‘we two’ (‘wit’) and ‘of us two’ (‘uncer’) besides the plural, here the king and queen. ‘uncran’ and ‘eaferan’ are accusative plural (‘eaferan’ is a weak noun, whose dative plural would end in ‘-um’), the object of ‘gyldan’, so ‘repay our offspring’, our sons as a group. ‘gif hē þæt eal gemon’ is ‘if he remembers all that’ (‘gemon’ the third singular present of ‘gemunan’). The clause ‘hwæt wit … gefremedon’ says what: ‘hwæt’ is ‘what’ (accusative neuter), ‘wit’ the dual ‘we two’, ‘gefremedon’ the past plural of ‘gefremman’, ‘to do’. ‘tō willan ond tō worðmyndum’ is ‘for his pleasure and his honours’ (‘worðmynd’, honour, dative plural). ‘ārna’ is the genitive plural of ‘ār’, ‘of kindnesses’, depending on ‘hwæt’. ‘umbọrwesendum’ is found only here; it is ‘umbor’ (child) with ‘wesende’ (being), and I take it as ‘while he was a child’, though no noun or pronoun in the dative stands beside it for the participle to agree with, which is odd for one child. This is a guess from the parts. The dot under the ‘ọ’ is again Klaeber’s metrical sign. The closing quotation mark ends Wealhtheow’s speech.

sentences.l: She turned then by the bench, where her sons were, Hrethric and Hrothmund, and the sons of heroes, the youth together;
sentences.i: Then she went to the bench, where her sons were, Hrethric and Hrothmund, and the sons of warriors, the young men together;
sentences.n: ‘Hwearf’ is the past singular of ‘hweorfan’, ‘to turn, go’, and the unstated subject is Wealhtheow. ‘bī bence’ is ‘by the bench’ (dative singular), ‘þǣr’ is ‘where’, and ‘hyre byre’ is ‘her sons’ (‘hyre’ ‘her’, ‘byre’ ‘sons’, nominative plural), with ‘wǣron’ ‘were’. ‘Hrēðrīc ond Hrōðmund’ names them, and ‘hæleþa bearn’ is ‘sons of heroes’ (genitive plural ‘hæleþa’), presumably the sons of the other noblemen in the hall. ‘giogoð ætgædere’ is ‘youth together’ (‘giogoð’, nominative, a collective for young men); the sentence continues the picture of the queen moving through the hall, after her speech to the king.

sentences.t:
þǣr se gōda sæt,
Bēowulf Gēata be þǣm gebrōðrum twǣm.
sentences.l: where the good one sat, Beowulf of the Geats, by the two brothers.
sentences.i: where the good man sat, Beowulf of the Geats, beside the two brothers.
sentences.n: ‘þǣr se gōda sæt’ is ‘where the good one sat’: ‘se gōda’ is the weak adjective with the article used as a noun, ‘the good one’, and ‘Bēowulf Gēata’ (‘of the Geats’, genitive plural) names him in apposition. ‘be þǣm gebrōðrum twǣm’ is ‘by the two brothers’, with ‘be’ governing the dative: ‘þǣm’, ‘gebrōðrum’ and ‘twǣm’ are all dative plural. The brothers are Hrethric and Hrothmund, and this puts Beowulf next to Hrothgar’s sons, the pair in whose favour the queen has just spoken.
